claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to phase separation under high thermal and irradiation stress.
Untreated W–Cu composites are prone to interfacial void formation under high thermal and irradiation stress.
A thin, conformal Ti/Ni coating should be deposited on W particles or ligaments by magnetron sputtering before consolidation.
The Ti/Ni coating forms a stable interfacial layer between W and Cu.
The Ti/Ni interfacial layer bridges the chemical and physical mismatch between W and Cu.
The Ti/Ni coating reduces interfacial void nucleation.
The Ti/Ni coating suppresses phase separation.
The Ti/Ni coating acts as a diffusion barrier at the W/Cu interface.
The Ti/Ni coating enhances metallurgical bonding at the W/Cu interface.
During thermal cycling and irradiation, the coating limits interdiffusion between W and Cu.
Limiting W–Cu interdiffusion allows interfacial strain to be relieved without producing voids.
The coating produces a more coherent interface that preserves thermal-conduction pathways.
Ti/Ni-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than uncoated W–Cu composites after relevant heat-transfer and irradiation exposure.
Suppression of interfacial voids and phase separation is responsible for the predicted thermal-conductivity improvement.
Interfacial void formation and phase separation degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The intervention is applicable to fusion-component joint regions where W-based plasma-facing material meets Cu-based cooling assemblies.
